paragraphs: These are the tribes and their territories: Dan gets one portion, along the northern boundary. It follows the Hethlon road that turns off toward the entrance of Hamath, as far as Hazor-enon. The territory of Damascus lies to the north, alongside Hamath. The northern border stretches from east to west.
Asher gets one portion, bordering Dan from east to west.
Naphtali gets one portion, bordering Asher from east to west.
Manasseh gets one portion, bordering Naphtali from east to west.
Ephraim gets one portion, bordering Manasseh from east to west.
Reuben gets one portion, bordering Ephraim from east to west.
Judah gets one portion, bordering Reuben from east to west.

Bordering Judah from east to west is the consecrated area that you will set apart as holy. It's a square, roughly seven miles by seven miles, with the Sanctuary right at the center. The area reserved for God is seven miles long and a little less than three miles wide.

This is how it will be divided up. The priests get the area measuring seven miles on the north and south sides, with a width of a little more than three miles on the east and west sides. The Sanctuary of God will be at the center. This is for the consecrated priests, the Zadokites who stayed faithful in their service to me and didn't wander off track the way the Levites did when Israel went astray. This is their special gift, a gift from the land itself, most holy ground, bordering the Levites' section.
The Levites get a section equal in size to the priests', roughly seven miles by three miles. They're not allowed to sell or trade any of it. It's the best part of the land, and it's holy to God.

What's left of the 'sacred square'—each side measures about seven miles by a mile and a half—is for ordinary use: the city and its buildings, with open country around it, but the city at the center. The north, south, east, and west sides of the city are each about a mile and a half long. A strip of pasture, about 125 yards wide, will surround the city on all sides. The rest of this portion, three miles of countryside to the east and west of the sacred area, is for farming. It will provide food for the city. Workers from all the tribes of Israel will work the fields and farm the land.
This dedicated area, set apart for holy purposes, will be a square, seven miles by seven miles—a 'holy square'—which includes the part set aside for the city.

The rest of this land, the country stretching east to the Jordan River and west to the Mediterranean Sea from the seven-mile sides of the 'holy square,' belongs to the prince. His land sits between the tribal territories to the north and south, extending east and west from the 'sacred square' with its Temple at the center. The land set aside for the Levites on one side and the city on the other sits in the middle of the prince's territory. The 'sacred square' is flanked on the east and west by the prince's land, and bordered on the north and south by the territories of Judah and Benjamin.
And then the rest of the tribes: Benjamin gets one portion, stretching from the eastern to the western boundary.
Simeon gets one portion, bordering Benjamin from east to west.
Issachar gets one portion, bordering Simeon from east to west.
Zebulun gets one portion, bordering Issachar from east to west.
Gad gets one portion, bordering Zebulun from east to west.
The southern boundary of Gad will run south from Tamar to the waters of Meribah-kadesh, along the Brook of Egypt, and then out to the Great Mediterranean Sea.
This is the land you are to divide among the tribes of Israel as their inheritance. These are their portions. This is the decree of God, the Master.

These are the gates of the city. On the north side, which is 2,250 yards long (the city gates are named after the tribes of Israel), there are three gates: the gate of Reuben, the gate of Judah, and the gate of Levi.
On the east side, measuring 2,250 yards, three gates: the gate of Joseph, the gate of Benjamin, and the gate of Dan.
On the south side, measuring 2,250 yards, three gates: the gate of Simeon, the gate of Issachar, and the gate of Zebulun.
On the west side, measuring 2,250 yards, three gates: the gate of Gad, the gate of Asher, and the gate of Naphtali.
The four sides of the city add up to nearly six miles in total. From now on, the name of the city will be Yahweh-Shammah, which means 'God-Is-There.'
title: The Sanctuary of God at the Center
